items.prompt: Gross domestic product (GDP) is best defined as:

options.label: The total money held by households and firms in a country at one point in time
The market value of final goods and services produced within a country in a period
The value of all goods and services a country's citizens buy anywhere in the world
The difference between what a country's government collects and what it spends

rubric: GDP counts final goods and services produced inside a country's borders over a period.
Distractors confuse GDP with the money supply, with spending by citizens abroad, or with the budget balance.

items.prompt: What does the term inflation refer to?

options.label: An increase in the total amount of goods an economy produces each year
A fall in the value of a country's stock market over several months
A rise in the price of one popular product because demand increased
A sustained rise in the general level of prices across the economy

rubric: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level.
Distractors confuse it with a stock fall, a single relative price change, or economic growth.

items.prompt: The unemployment rate is the percentage of the:

options.label: Total population that does not currently have a paid job
Employed workers who changed employers during the past year
Labour force that is without a job and actively looking for work
Working-age population that has never held a job in their lifetime

rubric: The rate is unemployed people actively seeking work divided by the labour force.
Distractors use the whole population, lifetime history, or job switching instead of the labour force definition.

items.prompt: Which of the following is a tool of monetary policy?

options.label: Increasing government spending on roads and schools
Changing the central bank's target interest rate
Placing a tariff on imported steel to protect producers
Changing the rate of income tax paid by households

rubric: Monetary policy is run by the central bank, mainly via interest rates.
Distractors are fiscal (taxes, spending) or trade policy tools.

items.prompt: Fiscal policy refers to a government's use of:

options.label: Wage and price controls to hold down living costs
Government spending and taxation to influence the economy
Tariffs and quotas to regulate trade with other countries
Interest rates and the money supply to steer the economy

rubric: Fiscal policy is government spending and taxation.
Distractors describe monetary policy, trade policy, or price controls.

items.prompt: Which of the following are components of GDP in the expenditure approach (C + I + G + NX)? Select all that apply.

options.label: Pension and welfare transfer payments
Net exports (exports minus imports)
Household consumption
Business investment
Purchases of existing shares on the stock market

rubric: The expenditure approach sums consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports.
Transfer payments and share trading are not spending on newly produced output.

items.prompt: A news report says a country's real GDP shrank in each of the last two consecutive quarters. The presenter says the country has entered a particular phase of the business cycle. Which term is commonly used for this?

options.label: Hyperinflation
Stagnation of trade
Expansion
Recession

rubric: Two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP is the common rule of thumb for a recession.
Expansion is the opposite; hyperinflation concerns prices, not output.

items.prompt: Why do economists prefer real GDP to nominal GDP when comparing output across years?

options.label: Real GDP is measured only in the base year, so it never changes
Real GDP removes the effect of price changes, so it reflects changes in quantity produced
Real GDP leaves out government spending, which distorts comparisons
Real GDP includes imports, so it shows total national spending

rubric: Real GDP holds prices constant so that changes reflect output, not inflation.
Distractors invent differences in what is included or misdescribe the base year.

items.prompt: If a central bank raises its policy interest rate, what is the most likely effect on the economy?

options.label: Imports become cheaper because prices fall, so the trade deficit shrinks quickly
Government tax revenue rises immediately, which funds more public spending
Borrowing becomes costlier, spending slows, and inflation pressure eases
Borrowing becomes cheaper, spending rises, and unemployment tends to fall

rubric: Higher rates raise borrowing costs, dampening demand and inflation.
The second option describes a rate cut; the others assume unrelated mechanisms.

items.prompt: A factory closes because robots now do the work, and its former employees lack the skills for the jobs available locally. Which type of unemployment is this?

options.label: Frictional unemployment, from normal time spent between jobs
Seasonal unemployment, from predictable yearly changes in work
Cyclical unemployment, from a downturn in overall demand
Structural unemployment, from a mismatch between skills and available jobs

rubric: A skills mismatch caused by technological change is structural unemployment.
Frictional is short job search; cyclical follows recessions; seasonal follows the calendar.

items.prompt: A consumer price index rises from 200 to 210 over one year. What does this tell you?

options.label: Prices fell by 5 percent, since the index moved by ten points
Inflation was 5 percent, since prices rose by 10 on a base of 200
Inflation was 10 percent, since the index rose by ten points
Real output grew by 10 percent, since the index went up

rubric: Inflation is the percentage change: (210-200)/200 = 5 percent.
Distractors confuse points with percent or link the index to output.

items.prompt: What is the most direct effect of a new tariff on imported cars in the importing country?

options.label: Foreign car makers must cut their home prices to match the tax
Domestic buyers pay higher prices for imported cars than before
Exports of the country's own goods automatically increase in response
Domestic car prices fall as local firms face less competition

rubric: A tariff is a tax on imports, raising their domestic price.
Distractors reverse the price effect or assume automatic export gains.

items.prompt: A government responds to a recession with expansionary fiscal policy (more spending and lower taxes). Which effects would economists expect? Select all that apply.

options.label: Aggregate demand increases
The budget deficit tends to widen
Real output rises and unemployment tends to fall
Inflation pressure necessarily disappears
Aggregate demand falls as households save more

rubric: Spending and tax cuts raise demand and output but reduce the budget balance.
Falling demand and vanishing inflation pressure contradict the expansionary effect.

items.prompt: A country's currency loses value against its trading partners' currencies over a year. Foreign buyers now need fewer units of their own money to buy the country's wheat, while imported electronics cost locals more. What is the most likely effect on the country's trade?

options.label: Trade stays the same because exchange rates only affect tourism
Exports tend to fall and imports rise, since the currency is weaker
Both exports and imports fall because all trade becomes more expensive
Exports tend to rise and imports tend to fall, improving the trade balance

rubric: Depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home, raising net exports.
Other options reverse the effect or deny exchange rates affect goods trade.

items.prompt: Why do economists compare real GDP rather than nominal GDP when judging growth across several years?

options.label: Real GDP uses current prices each year, so it reflects today's costs
Real GDP counts only goods sold abroad, so it shows trade strength
Real GDP adds black-market activity, so it shows the full economy
Real GDP removes the effect of price changes, so it shows changes in output

rubric: Real GDP holds prices constant, so changes reflect output rather than inflation.
Nominal GDP can rise from price increases alone, which the current-price distractor overlooks.

items.prompt: A factory installs robots and lays off its assembly workers, whose skills no longer match the jobs available locally. What type of unemployment is this?

options.label: Seasonal
Frictional
Structural
Cyclical

rubric: Structural unemployment comes from a mismatch between workers' skills and available jobs.
Cyclical is the common wrong pick, but it is tied to the business cycle, not technology change.

items.prompt: A central bank raises its main policy interest rate. What is the most likely effect on the economy?

options.label: Loans become costlier, so spending and investment slow and inflation pressure eases
Loans become cheaper, so spending slows as people save less
Loans become costlier, so spending speeds up as people rush to borrow
Loans become cheaper, so firms hire more and the currency weakens

rubric: Higher rates raise borrowing costs, which dampens spending and eases inflation.
Distractors confuse the direction of the rate effect on borrowing or on spending.

items.prompt: A news report says the annual inflation rate fell from 6% to 3%. What does this mean?

options.label: Prices have dropped by half compared with last year
Prices are now falling, back toward last year's level
Prices are stable, so the cost of living no longer rises
Prices are still rising, but more slowly than before

rubric: Disinflation means prices still rise, but at a slower rate.
Distractors confuse a lower inflation rate with falling prices (deflation).

items.prompt: Why are unemployment benefits described as an automatic stabilizer?

options.label: Payments are fixed by law at one level, so they never change spending
Payments are set each year by the central bank to steer interest rates
Payments are cut in a downturn, which forces the budget into balance
Payments rise in a downturn without new legislation, cushioning demand

rubric: Benefit spending rises automatically when unemployment rises, supporting demand.
Distractors confuse automatic stabilizers with discretionary or monetary policy.

items.prompt: Which of the following are examples of fiscal policy? Select all that apply.

options.label: The government cuts income tax rates
The central bank lowers its policy interest rate
The central bank buys government bonds
The government increases spending on road building

rubric: Fiscal policy is government taxation and spending.
Bond purchases and policy rate changes are monetary policy run by the central bank.

items.prompt: A news report says a country's currency has depreciated 10% against its trading partners. A local furniture maker exports most of its output, and a local shop imports electronics. What is the most likely effect?

options.label: Furniture becomes pricier for foreign buyers, while imported electronics cost less locally
Both furniture exports and electronics imports become cheaper for everyone
Neither price changes, because exchange rates affect only financial assets
Furniture becomes cheaper for foreign buyers, while imported electronics cost more locally

rubric: A weaker currency makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home.
Strongest distractor reverses the direction, mixing up depreciation with appreciation.

items.prompt: Nominal GDP grew 7% over a year, while the GDP deflator rose 4%. Approximately how much did real GDP grow?

options.label: About 4%
About 11%
About 3%
About 7%

rubric: Real growth is roughly nominal growth minus inflation: 7% - 4% = 3%.
Adding the rates or ignoring prices are common slips.

items.prompt: An economy has 300 million adults aged 16+, of whom 180 million are employed, 20 million are unemployed and looking for work, and 100 million are not in the labour force. What is the unemployment rate?
rubric: Unemployment rate = unemployed / labour force = 20 / 200 = 10%.
6.7% wrongly divides by all adults; 11.1% divides by employed only.

items.prompt: The consumer price index was 250 last year and is 260 this year. What was the inflation rate?
rubric: 3.8% divides by the new index, and 10% reports the raw index change.

items.prompt: The marginal propensity to consume is 0.8. The government raises spending by 10 billion. Using the simple spending multiplier, what is the total increase in output?

options.label: 8 billion
12.5 billion
50 billion
40 billion

rubric: Multiplier = 1 / (1 - 0.8) = 5, so 10 x 5 = 50 billion.
Other options misuse MPC or divide instead of using the multiplier.

items.prompt: An economy has 9% unemployment, 1% inflation and output well below its potential. Which policy mix best fits this situation?

options.label: Cut taxes and lower the policy interest rate to lift demand
Raise taxes and lower the policy interest rate to cut debt
Raise taxes and lift the policy interest rate to cool demand
Cut government spending and lift the policy interest rate

rubric: A recession gap with low inflation calls for expansionary fiscal and monetary policy.
Distractors apply contractionary policy, suited to overheating economies.

items.prompt: Which of these events would, other things equal, shift aggregate demand to the right? Select all that apply.

options.label: The government cuts income taxes
The central bank raises interest rates
The government cuts its own spending
Household confidence rises and people spend more
Foreign demand for the country's exports rises

rubric: Higher consumption, tax cuts and stronger exports all raise aggregate demand.
Higher rates and spending cuts reduce aggregate demand.

items.prompt: An economist is computing GDP by the expenditure approach for a small country. Consumption is 600, investment is 150, government spending is 200, exports are 100 and imports are 120 (all in billions). What is GDP?

options.label: 950 billion
930 billion
1,050 billion
1,070 billion

rubric: Distractors ignore trade, ignore imports, or add imports instead of subtracting.

items.prompt: An economy's nominal GDP grows from 2,000 to 2,200 billion while the GDP deflator rises from 100 to 108. Approximately what is real GDP growth?

options.label: About 10%
About 1.9%
About 8%
About 18%

rubric: Distractors use nominal growth (10%) or the price change (8%) or add them.

items.prompt: The marginal propensity to consume is 0.75 and the government raises spending by 40 billion, with no taxes changing and no crowding out. By how much does equilibrium GDP rise using the simple spending multiplier?

options.label: 160 billion
120 billion
53 billion
40 billion

rubric: 120 uses MPC x spending; 53 divides by MPC wrongly; 40 ignores the multiplier.

items.prompt: Using the Fisher relation, a bank offers a nominal interest rate of 6% while expected inflation is 2.5%. What is the approximate expected real interest rate?
rubric: Real rate ≈ nominal minus expected inflation = 3.5%.
8.5% adds inflation instead of subtracting it.

items.prompt: A country has 150 million working-age people, of whom 90 million are employed and 10 million are unemployed and looking for work. The rest are not in the labour force. What is the unemployment rate?
rubric: Labour force = 100 million; 10/100 = 10%.
11.1% divides by employed; 6.7% divides by working-age population.

items.prompt: A central bank wants to reduce inflation using open market operations. Which action fits that goal?

options.label: Lower the reserve requirement ratio for banks
Cut the interest rate paid on reserves to zero
Sell government bonds to banks, reducing reserves
Buy government bonds from banks, raising reserves

rubric: Selling bonds drains reserves, tightening credit and lowering demand.
Buying bonds or lowering requirements expand money and credit.

items.prompt: Which of the following transactions are counted in this year's GDP of a country? Select all that apply.

options.label: A newly built house sold by a developer
A haircut bought from a local salon
Sale of a used car from one household to another
Stock market purchase of existing company shares

rubric: GDP counts newly produced final goods and services this year.
Used goods and financial asset transfers are not new production.

items.prompt: An economy is in a deep recession with high unemployment and idle capacity, and the central bank's policy rate is already near zero. Policymakers want to raise output quickly. Which step would the standard Keynesian model recommend?

options.label: Raise income tax rates to reduce the deficit
Impose import quotas to cut imports while cutting spending
Increase government spending financed by borrowing
Cut the central bank's policy rate further below zero by decree of the treasury

rubric: With monetary policy constrained, fiscal expansion raises aggregate demand.
Tax hikes and spending cuts would deepen the recession.

items.prompt: Prices rise 6% while output falls and unemployment increases after a sudden jump in global oil prices. Which diagnosis best fits?

options.label: A negative supply shock shifting short-run aggregate supply left
An expansionary monetary policy shifting aggregate demand right
A productivity improvement shifting long-run supply right
A demand-pull boom from rising consumer confidence

rubric: Higher prices with falling output signals stagflation from a supply shock.
Demand increases would raise output and employment along with prices.

items.prompt: A government cuts taxes and the central bank keeps its money supply fixed. Interest rates rise and private investment falls somewhat. Which mechanism explains this?

options.label: Exchange rates fix investment regardless of interest rates
The multiplier raises saving so interest rates always fall
Crowding out: borrowing raises money demand and interest rates
Lower taxes cut aggregate demand through lower disposable income

rubric: Higher deficits and spending increase money demand, raising rates and reducing investment.
The other options reverse the direction of the effects.

items.prompt: A country's currency depreciates by 15% and, one year later, the trade deficit is initially larger before shrinking over time. What best explains this pattern?

options.label: Import and export volumes adjust slowly, so the price effect dominates at first
Exports always fall after depreciation because foreign goods are cheaper
Trade balances do not respond to exchange rates at all
Depreciation makes imports cheaper, so volumes rise immediately

rubric: The J-curve: prices change fast, quantities adjust slowly.
Distractors misstate the direction of price effects or deny responsiveness.

items.prompt: Headline inflation is 5% but core inflation (excluding food and energy) is 2%. Which interpretation is best supported?

options.label: Underlying demand pressure is stronger than the headline rate shows
The gap means the central bank has lost control of money supply
Temporary food and energy price swings are probably driving the gap
Core inflation is wrong because it ignores the cost of living

rubric: Core strips volatile items, so a large gap points to food and energy shocks.
The distractors misread what core measures.

items.prompt: Unemployment falls from 7% to 5% over two years, yet the labour force participation rate also drops sharply. Why should an analyst be cautious about reading this as a stronger labour market?

options.label: Discouraged workers leaving the labour force lower the rate without new jobs
Lower participation raises the number of unemployed counted
Participation changes never affect the unemployment rate
Falling unemployment always means more people are employed

rubric: Only people actively seeking work count as unemployed, so exits shrink the rate.
Other options misstate the measurement link.

items.prompt: A central bank raises its policy rate sharply. Which effects would an analyst expect to see as the transmission works through the economy? Select all that apply.

options.label: Higher borrowing costs reduce investment and durable goods spending
Currency tends to appreciate as foreign capital seeks higher returns
Net exports tend to rise because domestic goods get cheaper abroad
Mortgage payments and credit costs generally fall

rubric: Rate hikes dampen interest-sensitive spending and attract capital, appreciating the currency.
Appreciation would lower net exports, not raise them.

items.prompt: A government finances a large tax cut by borrowing, and households anticipate future tax rises to repay the debt, so they save nearly all of the extra income. Consumption barely changes. Which concept best explains why the policy had little effect?

options.label: Ricardian equivalence: forward-looking households offset the deficit with saving
The liquidity trap: interest rates are too high to encourage spending
Purchasing power parity: exchange rates restore equal prices
The paradox of toil: higher wages always cut employment

rubric: Ricardian equivalence says debt-financed tax cuts are saved in expectation of later taxes.
The other concepts concern different mechanisms.

items.prompt: Nominal GDP grew 6% over a year. The GDP deflator rose 4% and CPI rose 2.5%. Which estimate of real GDP growth is most appropriate, and why?

options.label: About 1.5%, because CPI and deflator should be averaged to remove bias
About 3.5%, because CPI is the standard measure of price changes for households
About 2%, because the deflator covers all domestically produced output in GDP
About 10%, because real growth is nominal growth plus the inflation rate

rubric: Real GDP growth is roughly nominal growth minus the GDP deflator, about 2%, since the deflator covers all output.
Using CPI confuses a consumer basket with the whole output basket; adding inflation reverses the sign.

items.prompt: The unemployment rate falls from 6.0% to 5.5%, yet the employment-to-population ratio is unchanged. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: The statistics agency changed how it values part-time work in the ratio
Labour force participation fell, as some jobless people stopped searching
Frictional unemployment fell as job matching improved across industries
Firms hired many more workers, but population growth masked the gain

rubric: If employment relative to population is flat but unemployment fell, people left the labour force.
Hiring-based explanations would raise the employment ratio; matching improvements would also show up in employment.

items.prompt: A central bank holds its nominal policy rate at 4% for two years. Over that time inflation falls from 5% to 3%. What happened to policy stance, other things equal?

options.label: Policy tightened, since the real rate rose from about -1% to about +1%
Policy stayed neutral because the nominal rate did not change at all
Policy tightened only if the exchange rate also appreciated over the period
Policy loosened because falling inflation reduces the burden of debt

rubric: The real rate is the nominal rate minus inflation, so it rose by about two points, a passive tightening.
A fixed nominal rate is not a fixed stance; the exchange rate is not required for the real rate to change.

items.prompt: The government raises spending by 2% of GDP. The economy is at full capacity and the central bank, targeting inflation, raises rates in response. Why is the observed output effect much smaller than a simple multiplier predicts?

options.label: Households save the entire increase in income, so spending cannot be passed on
Government spending has no effect on output once taxes are expected to rise
The multiplier only applies to tax cuts and not to direct government purchases
Higher rates and capacity limits crowd out private spending, offsetting the stimulus

rubric: At full capacity with an offsetting central bank, crowding out of private demand shrinks the multiplier.
Distractors assume full Ricardian offset, confuse spending with tax cuts, or assume a 100% saving rate.

items.prompt: A country's budget deficit widens by 3% of GDP while private saving and private investment stay unchanged. Using the saving-investment identity, what follows for the external position?

options.label: The current account moves toward surplus, as domestic demand is stronger
The current account deficit widens, as national saving falls short of investment
Nothing changes, because the budget and trade balances are independent
The capital account must move into deficit to finance higher government debt

rubric: National saving minus investment equals the current account balance, so lower public saving widens the deficit.
Treating the two deficits as unrelated, or reversing the capital flow direction, ignores the identity.

items.prompt: An economy sees consumer prices rising quickly. Which observations point to a cost-push supply shock rather than demand-pull inflation? Select all that apply.

options.label: Energy and input prices lead the increase in prices across sectors
Credit growth and retail sales are surging across all categories
Output is flat or falling while the price level rises
Output and employment are rising above trend while prices rise broadly
Unemployment is rising alongside the inflation

rubric: A supply shock raises prices while output falls and unemployment rises, with input prices leading.
Rising output, employment, credit and sales across the board suggest excess demand.

items.prompt: After a drought, headline inflation in a country reaches 8%, while core inflation (excluding food and energy) is 3% and wage growth is moderate. Analysts disagree on what the gap shows. What is the most defensible reading?

options.label: Wage growth being moderate proves that the drought has had no effect on prices
Core is unreliable, so headline reflects true underlying demand pressure
The gap shows the central bank has lost control over inflation expectations
Headline inflation is mostly a temporary shock to volatile prices, with weak underlying demand pressure

rubric: A large headline-core gap with moderate wages points to a supply shock in volatile components, not broad demand pressure.
The other options dismiss core, misread wages, or assume expectations de-anchored without evidence.

items.prompt: A recession hits. Policymakers need stimulus that is fast, easily reversed, and reaches households likely to spend most of any extra income. Which option best meets these criteria?

options.label: Temporary cash transfers to lower-income households through existing payment systems
A cut in the top income tax rate to improve incentives for saving
A permanent cut in the corporate tax rate to raise investment returns
A multi-year highway programme with long planning and approval stages

rubric: Temporary transfers to low-income households are fast, reversible and have a high marginal propensity to consume.
Infrastructure is slow, permanent corporate cuts are not reversible, and top-rate cuts reach people who save more.

items.prompt: A minister says: "Financing the deficit by creating money is better than borrowing, since it creates no debt and costs nothing." Which critique is strongest?

options.label: Money creation is limited by the gold reserves held by the central bank
Money creation always lowers interest rates, which hurts savers unfairly
Money financing beyond growth in money demand raises inflation, a hidden tax on money holders
Money financing is legal only when the budget is balanced over the cycle

rubric: Excess money creation produces inflation (seigniorage), which taxes holders of money, so it is not costless.
The other options invent a gold constraint, a legal rule, or a guaranteed interest-rate effect.

items.prompt: A government plans a tariff to save 5,000 steel jobs. Criteria: total welfare, effects on downstream industries, and cost per job saved. Which judgement best fits the criteria?

options.label: Doubtful: higher input prices cut downstream jobs, and the cost per job saved often exceeds the wage
Adopt it, because any job saved outweighs higher prices paid by consumers
Adopt it, because trade deficits always shrink when imports are taxed
Reject it outright, because tariffs never change employment in any industry

rubric: Tariffs raise input costs for steel-using industries and consumers, so the cost per job saved is typically high.
The other options ignore costs, overstate the claim that tariffs never matter, or assume trade balances follow tariffs mechanically.

items.prompt: An oil price spike lifts headline inflation. Criteria: avoid de-anchoring inflation expectations, and avoid needless output loss. Surveys show long-run expectations are stable at target. Which response is best?

options.label: Raise rates sharply at once to push headline inflation under target quickly
Look through the first-round effect while monitoring expectations and wages closely
Adopt a price freeze on fuel so that measured inflation is held to target
Cut rates to offset the lost purchasing power that households experience

rubric: With anchored expectations, a central bank can look through a one-off supply shock while watching for second-round effects.
Sharp hikes cause unnecessary output loss, cuts risk de-anchoring, and price freezes distort without addressing the shock.

items.prompt: A small open commodity exporter faces volatile world prices for its main export, and has a record of low inflation. Criteria: absorb terms-of-trade shocks and keep credibility. Which regime is best?

options.label: A floating rate with inflation targeting, so the currency adjusts to export price swings
A crawling peg set to the previous year's inflation, whatever happens to commodity prices
A hard peg, because it removes exchange rate movements and so any need for adjustment
A currency board, since low past inflation shows that devaluation is never needed

rubric: A float lets the currency depreciate when export prices fall, cushioning the shock, and inflation targeting preserves credibility.
Pegs and boards shift the adjustment to wages, prices and employment; a past low inflation record does not remove shocks.

items.prompt: A country proposes a strict annual balanced-budget rule with no exceptions. Which are valid criticisms from a stabilisation perspective? Select all that apply.

options.label: It forces spending cuts or tax rises in recessions, which deepens the downturn
It guarantees lower interest rates on government bonds in every period
It makes monetary policy unnecessary because demand is always stable
It can discourage borrowing for investment with long-term returns
It disables automatic stabilisers such as unemployment benefits

rubric: A strict annual rule is procyclical, blocks automatic stabilisers and treats investment like consumption.
Neither stable demand nor guaranteed lower yields follows from such a rule.

items.prompt: A country has public debt of 120% of GDP, an average interest rate of 2% and trend nominal growth of 3%, and runs a primary balance of zero. A think tank urges immediate sharp austerity to stabilise debt. Criteria: debt sustainability and avoiding needless output loss. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Austerity is essential, because any debt above 100% of GDP is unsustainable
Austerity is needed, because a zero primary balance means debt rises each year
The debt ratio is already falling since growth exceeds interest, so a modest buffer beats sharp austerity
Debt is irrelevant, because the government can always print currency to repay it

rubric: When growth exceeds the interest rate and the primary balance is zero, the debt ratio drifts down, so sharp austerity is not justified, though a buffer guards against r rising.
The other options rely on a fixed threshold, a mistaken dynamic, or ignore inflation and financing risk.

items.prompt: An oil price spike lifts headline inflation to 7% while unemployment is 4%. Surveyed long-run inflation expectations have begun to drift up. The central bank's criteria: avoid a wage-price spiral and limit output loss. Which response fits best?

options.label: Tighten enough to show commitment to the target, accepting a modest output cost, since drifting expectations make second-round effects likely
Impose fuel price controls, since they lower measured headline inflation with no output cost and no effect on expectations at all
Look through the shock completely, since supply shocks are transitory and tightening would only cost output without changing oil prices at all
Cut the policy rate to offset lost real income, since the shock cuts demand and output far more than it raises prices at first

rubric: Drifting expectations raise the risk of second-round effects, so a measured tightening is justified under the stated criteria.
Look-through is right only when expectations stay anchored; rate cuts and price controls ignore the wage-price spiral risk.

items.prompt: A government cuts taxes with no change in spending, financed by bonds. Ricardian equivalence predicts no change in consumption. Which finding most undermines that prediction as a description of household behaviour?

options.label: Bond yields stay unchanged after the extra issue, so there is no visible crowding out of private investment in the economy
Wealthier households save most of the cut, since they expect future taxes to rise by a matching present-value amount
Many households are liquidity constrained and spend most extra current income, so their consumption rises when taxes are cut
Private saving rises by roughly the size of the cut, so national saving is unchanged and no extra demand appears in the economy

rubric: Liquidity-constrained households cannot smooth consumption against expected future taxes, which breaks the theory's key assumption.
The other options describe behaviour consistent with equivalence or irrelevant market outcomes.

items.prompt: A commentator says a persistent current account deficit of 4% of GDP proves the country's firms are uncompetitive, so imports should be restricted. Which critique is strongest?

options.label: Import restrictions would end the deficit permanently, since saving and investment decisions are unaffected by trade barriers in any case
Competitiveness never affects trade balances, since the central bank's policy interest rate alone fixes the current account over time
Deficits are harmless because the exchange rate adjusts automatically and removes any external imbalance within about a year every time
The deficit equals investment minus national saving, so it may reflect foreign finance of high-return investment, not weak export competitiveness

rubric: The identity CA = S - I shows the deficit can mirror strong investment funded from abroad, so competitiveness is not proven.
Other options overstate automatic adjustment, ignore saving-investment effects, or deny any role for competitiveness.

items.prompt: Judge in which setting a debt-financed rise in government spending would have the largest output multiplier, and why.

options.label: Floating exchange rate with high capital mobility, since the currency depreciates and net exports rise to add to the extra spending
Full employment with an inflation-targeting central bank, since the extra demand lifts output more when capacity use is already high
High public debt, since households expect lower future taxes and so spend all of the extra income they receive from the state
Policy rate at the zero lower bound, since the central bank does not raise rates in response and so real rates do not offset it

rubric: At the zero lower bound monetary policy does not offset the stimulus, so the multiplier is larger.
Under floating rates with mobile capital the currency tends to appreciate and crowd out net exports, and the other options reverse standard logic.

items.prompt: An economy is often hit by productivity shocks. Criteria for the monetary rule: keep long-run inflation expectations anchored and avoid forcing a deep output loss after a temporary fall in productivity. Which rule is best?

options.label: Strict targeting of quarterly headline inflation, since any deviation however brief destroys credibility and cannot be justified by supply shocks
Flexible inflation targeting with a medium-term horizon, letting inflation deviate briefly after supply shocks while committing to return to target
A fixed money growth rule, since it removes discretion and keeps both inflation and output stable whatever happens to velocity of money
A fixed exchange rate peg to a large economy, since it guarantees domestic productivity shocks will be absorbed without any output cost

rubric: A medium-term horizon trades off the two stated criteria: anchored expectations and limited output loss.
Strict quarterly targeting, money rules and pegs each ignore either the output cost or instability in money demand and shock transmission.

items.prompt: Which are valid reasons why the headline unemployment rate can understate labour market slack? Select all that apply.

options.label: It excludes people who left a job voluntarily during the survey period, however long they have been searching
Involuntary part-time workers who want full-time hours are counted as fully employed
The rate can fall because participation falls, even if no new jobs have been created
Discouraged workers who stop searching leave the labour force and are no longer counted as unemployed
It counts retirees and full-time students as unemployed, which inflates the measured level of slack

rubric: Discouraged workers, involuntary part-timers and falling participation all hide slack in the headline rate.
Retirees and students are outside the labour force, and voluntary leavers who search are counted as unemployed.

items.prompt: A small economy pegs its currency to a large neighbour's and allows free capital flows. Strong inflows have pushed credit growth to 20% a year and inflation to 6%, while the anchor country's interest rates are low. Criteria: keep the peg, curb overheating, limit financial risk. Which response is best?

options.label: Cut taxes to support households, since lower disposable income is the main cause of the overheating in a pegged economy
Tighten fiscal policy and impose macroprudential limits on credit, since interest rates are tied to the anchor under the peg
Float the currency immediately, since that is the only way to cut inflation and carries no transition cost or risk of volatility
Raise the policy rate far above the anchor's, since a pegged central bank keeps full control of domestic rates despite open capital flows

rubric: With a peg and open capital, rates follow the anchor, so fiscal and macroprudential tools must curb overheating.
Raising rates draws more inflows, floating drops the peg criterion, and tax cuts add to demand.

items.prompt: A central bank must respond to persistent inflation, not transitory energy swings, yet stay accountable to a public that sees headline prices. Which framework design meets both constraints?

options.label: Target headline inflation each month and adjust rates after every energy price move, so that the public always sees an immediate response
Target headline inflation over a stated medium-term horizon, steer using core and trimmed-mean measures, and publish explanations of deviations
Target core inflation only and stop publishing headline forecasts, since the public needs to hear only the measure the bank controls
Target the price of a fixed basket of energy goods, since their volatility is the main source of the public's inflation worries

rubric: A headline target with a medium-term horizon, guided by underlying measures and explained deviations meets accountability and persistence.
Core-only targeting weakens accountability; monthly reaction chases transitory shocks; an energy target misses the aim.

items.prompt: Design a fiscal rule with three constraints: debt stays sustainable, automatic stabilisers can work in recessions, and governments cannot easily game it. Which design meets all three?

options.label: A ban on all new borrowing, with exceptions granted by the finance minister whenever a recession is declared by the government
A cap on the actual annual deficit of 3% of GDP, enforced by automatic spending cuts whenever revenues fall short in any year
A promise to balance the budget at the end of each parliament, with the government's own forecasts used to judge compliance
A structural (cyclically adjusted) balance rule with a debt ceiling anchor, reviewed by an independent fiscal council that checks the forecasts

rubric: Structural targets let stabilisers operate, the debt anchor secures sustainability, and an independent council limits gaming.
Actual deficit caps are procyclical; self-assessed forecasts and ministerial exceptions invite manipulation.

items.prompt: A government proposes a currency board to end high inflation: fix the exchange rate to the dollar, keep the capital account open, and let the treasury continue to borrow freely from the central bank. Which essential element is the proposal missing?

options.label: A higher fixed rate than the market rate, so exports are cheaper and the external balance improves without any other measures
A rule that base money is fully backed by foreign reserves, ending central bank financing of the treasury and so making the peg credible
A ban on foreign banks, so domestic lenders cannot move deposits abroad when confidence falls and the peg is under pressure
A floating band around the peg wide enough to let the rate absorb any shock, with no commitment to a central parity at all

rubric: A currency board needs reserve backing and no monetary financing of deficits, or the peg will not be credible.
The other options undermine credibility, ignore the flaw, or abandon the peg.

items.prompt: In a deep recession with the policy rate at zero and high public debt, design stimulus meeting these constraints: fast, temporary, high multiplier, no lasting rise in the deficit. Which package fits?

options.label: Permanent cuts in top income tax rates, since higher earners invest the money and the extra output pays for the lost revenue later
Temporary transfers to liquidity-constrained households and aid to states, with an automatic sunset when unemployment falls below a set level
A multi-year infrastructure programme starting in three years, since long projects add the most to future productive capacity and growth
A one-off money-financed cheque to every household, with the central bank pledging to keep the policy rate at zero for a decade

rubric: Temporary targeted transfers reach high-propensity spenders quickly and end by rule, meeting all four constraints.
Permanent cuts and delayed projects fail on speed or temporariness, and the cheque plan adds a lasting commitment.

items.prompt: A researcher wants to estimate the output effect of government spending while avoiding the problem that spending rises in response to the economy. Which research design best achieves this?

options.label: Compare countries with high and low spending shares, since cross-country differences are unrelated to their growth prospects or cycles
Use narrative-identified spending changes, such as military buildups driven by geopolitical events, as exogenous variation in spending
Regress output growth on actual spending growth across years, since larger samples average out the influence of the business cycle
Regress spending on past output, then interpret the coefficient as the effect of spending on output in the following year

rubric: Narrative or event-driven spending changes are plausibly unrelated to current output, which addresses reverse causality.
Simple regressions and cross-country comparisons stay confounded, and regressing spending on output reverses the question.

items.prompt: A commodity exporter wants a sovereign fund design that smooths government spending, limits real exchange rate appreciation, and avoids spending windfalls that may not last. Which design elements help meet these goals? Select all that apply.

options.label: Invest the saved revenue mainly in foreign assets, so spending the windfall does not push up domestic prices
Set the budget using a long-run reference commodity price and save revenue above it in the fund
Cap annual withdrawals at a fixed share of fund value, set by a published rule
Invest the fund in domestic property and local firms, since keeping the money at home supports growth
Spend all windfall revenue in the year received, so citizens gain from the boom before prices fall

rubric: A reference price, foreign investment and a withdrawal rule smooth spending and limit appreciation.
Spending everything or investing at home increases procyclicality and appreciation pressure.

items.prompt: A small open economy has 9% inflation after a depreciation raised import prices. Wages are indexed, expectations have drifted up, and the central bank has lost credibility. The aim: disinflate with a modest output loss. Which package best meets this?

options.label: Announce a credible target path backed by central bank independence and a consistent fiscal plan, and phase out wage indexation
Freeze prices and wages for a year, since controls remove inflation immediately and do not distort relative prices or supply
Raise rates sharply for one quarter and then cut, since a short sharp shock resets expectations without any wider institutional changes
Keep policy unchanged and wait for the depreciation effect to fade, since imported inflation is temporary and expectations cannot change

rubric: Credibility through independence, fiscal consistency and ending indexation lowers the sacrifice ratio by shifting expectations.
A brief shock lacks credibility, controls distort and fail, and waiting ignores de-anchored expectations.
